You’ve spent months training for your fall marathon, so the thought of losing that hard-earned fitness after race day probably stings. But at the same time, you can’t simply continue logging miles and workouts like you’re in race mode. Trying to stay razor-sharp year-round can lead to injury and burnout; your body needs rest after training for peak fitness.
So, instead, put your marathon fitness on ice. Freeze the adaptations you’ve gained and the endurance you’ve built. Then, you can pick up where you left off on, say, January 1, or whenever it’s time to lock back in for a spring marathon.
If you train right in the weeks between now and the new year, you won’t feel like you’re rebuilding fitness from scratch. Instead, you’ll preserve the key aerobic, muscular, and endurance adaptations you’ve worked so hard to develop.
To do that, we explain the minimum miles you need for maintenance and how speed, strength, and cross-training keep you in prime condition. Expect to return to race training feeling well-rested, confident, and ready to tackle another marathon cycle this spring.
How Many Miles Do I Need to Run Each Week?
In the first two weeks immediately following your marathon, you’ll want to focus more on rest and easy time-based jogging. Once you’ve recovered, however, you can return to tracking your miles more closely.
The bare minimum mileage you’ll need to maintain will vary from runner to runner, Heather Milton, CSCS, a clinical exercise physiologist and cofounder of Master My Run, tells Runner’s World. Much of it depends on how many miles you regularly put in over the weeks of your marathon training cycle.
“Science does not give us an exact number of what percentage of your marathon volume to decrease to that still allows you to maintain the same amount of aerobic fitness,” Milton explains. From her coaching experience, however, she’s found this number is likely around 50 percent of a runner’s typical weekly mileage.
David Hall, an RRCA- and USATF-certified run coach and founder of Running Coach CT, agrees. When planning his athletes’ schedules for the off-season, he looks at their typical running volume during marathon training and reduces their weekly mileage to no less than half. Every fourth week, however, mileage can drop to as low as 20 percent of their average to help facilitate recovery.
“A runner who was running 60 miles per week during their marathon build could definitely cut that in half,” Milton says. Or, take a runner who averaged around 40 miles per week. This individual could reduce their weekly mileage to 20, add in some cross-training, and expect to maintain much of their progress.
In fact, Milton adds, every runner can benefit from incorporating more of those cross-training sessions in the off-season. “Other forms of exercise can decrease the repetitiveness of the running motion and help you develop more well-rounded fitness, so I do prefer more variety from cross-training in the down-season,” she explains.
At the same time, Milton wants people to do the exercise they enjoy and, of course, runners love running. “I have to be reasonable about what a runner is willing to do and what keeps them healthy while they’re doing it,” she says. If you want to keep running four days per week in the off-season, that’s still workable—with one important caveat: You need to prioritize strength training.

I’ve since made running my job, and have had the opportunity to test dozens of running strollers over the years, and let me tell you, they are not all the same. The range of quality and ride between them can be pretty bananas, and as someone who tends toward higher mileage, it took me a long time to find one that I loved.
Thankfully, jogging strollers have evolved a lot since my first runs with my baby over a decade ago, and now there is a great jogging stroller for everyone no matter your height, running style, surfaces you run on, or miles you’ll be logging. Rachel Apa was nearing the end of her first New York City Marathon when she collapsed in Central Park on Sunday, November 1. The 24-year-old had spent months putting in the work needed to conquer 26.2 miles, but never made it across the finish line. Instead, she was taken to Mount Sinai Medical Center, where she died later that night.
Apa, a Bucknell University alum who lived in central Pennsylvania, came to New York to run with Parkinson's Foundation Champions, raising money in memory of her grandfather, who died from the disease in 2022.
According to reporting from The New York Times, the medical emergency happened around 1:30 p.m. close to Mile 24, around 85th Street, right as runners enter the final stretch through Central Park. Several spectators rushed to help and began performing CPR. New York Road Runners medical staff arrived shortly after, and tried to resuscitate her with a defibrillator before paramedics took her to the hospital.
Her parents had been keeping up with Rachel throughout the race as she made her way through the five boroughs, though from different locations. Michelle Apa, her mother, was in New York and watched Rachel run through Queens at Mile 14, while Steve Apa, her father, was back home in Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, following her progress through the marathon's tracking app.
Steve had been texting his daughter throughout the day. According to messages he shared with the Times, Rachel sent an "Ow" text at Mile 18, followed by a double "Ow ow" at Mile 19. She kept moving through the course, although her dad received no replies after that. As she reached Mile 23 on the app, Steve sent another message: "Final stretch." Rachel never responded.
Michelle eventually made her way to Central Park, reportedly arriving just as the ambulance carrying her daughter was leaving, per the Times. Doctors spent hours trying to save Rachel. Steve told the newspaper she was pronounced dead around 9:40 p.m.
"It's unfathomable," he told the newspaper. "Perfect health, perfect shape, 24 years old."
Steve told the Times that his daughter died from rhabdomyolysis, which occurs when damaged muscle tissue breaks down and releases substances into the bloodstream. The condition can cause serious kidney damage and, according to the Cleveland Clinic, can be triggered by extreme physical exertion.
An official cause of death had not been established as of Tuesday, November 3, with CBS New York reporting that the city's medical examiner was still investigating.
Sunday marked the marathon's first runner death following a medical incident since 2024, according to NYRR. The organization released a statement Monday:
"We are deeply saddened by the death of one of our runners following yesterday's race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with the runner's family, friends, and the entire running community."
Before the marathon, Apa explained her decision to run on her fundraising page, sharing how much her grandfather influenced her love of sports and why supporting the Parkinson's Foundation mattered to her.
"He taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement," she wrote.
Apa explained that watching him lose his mobility after his Parkinson's diagnosis had made her want to help others facing the disease. She wanted to use her first marathon to help others affected by it, raising money and awareness in the process “for research, better care, and a cure.”

One of the world's biggest marathons keeps getting bigger. On Sunday, November 1, the 2026 New York City Marathon officially cemented its place in the history books as the largest marathon of all time, surpassing the 2026 London Marathon, which had 59,830 finishers.
According to results released Monday by New York Road Runners (NYRR), 61,146 runners crossed the iconic finish line in Central Park (61,529 started the event). That total blasts past last year’s NYC tally of 59,226 finishers—which followed 2024’s record-breaking field of 55,646—marking the third consecutive year the five-borough race has raised the bar worldwide for mass participation.
This year’s record served as a nice topper for a historic run as it coincided with the 50th anniversary of the five-borough course. When organizers first took the race out of Central Park and onto the streets of Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Manhattan in 1976, the event was a bold urban experiment. Five decades later, it is an epicenter of the global running community, with waves of marathoners streaming from the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge from 8 a.m. until well after dark.
While tens of thousands of age-groupers, charity runners, and first-timers chased personal glory, the pro fields delivered plenty of fireworks at the front of the pack:
- A Historic Men’s Debut: Sweden’s Andreas Almgren broke the tape in 2:06:01 in his marathon debut, becoming the first Swedish runner to win any division in NYC Marathon history and the first man since Gebre Gebremariam in 2010 to win the open title in his 26.2-mile debut.
- Chepkirui Reclaims the Crown: Kenya’s Sheila Chepkirui captured her second NYC title in three years, clocking 2:24:36 to hold off a thrilling late charge.
- American Breakthroughs: Jess McClain threw down a gutsy final kick to take second in 2:24:42—just one second ahead of defending champion and course-record holder Hellen Obiri—becoming the first American woman to make the NYC open podium since Shalane Flanagan in 2018. On the men’s side, four Americans—led by sixth-place finisher Zouhair Talbi (2:06:43)—recorded the four fastest times ever run by U.S. men on the New York course.
- Swiss Wheelchair Dominance: Marcel Hug extended his own event record with an eighth men’s wheelchair victory (1:28:14), edging American Daniel Romanchuk by a single second, while Catherine Debrunner cruised to her second women’s title in 1:40:02.

The U.S. Capitol Building in Washington, D.C., on May 7, 2025 (Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom).
WASHINGTON — Voting ended Tuesday in this year’s midterm elections, leaving officials and volunteers counting tens of millions of ballots to determine which U.S. House and Senate candidates will take the oath of office in January.
The post-election process includes numerous steps and varying deadlines for when ballots have to be certified, since each state has different laws governing not only what happens on Election Day but what happens afterward.
Once local and state election officials wrap up their work, the process moves to Congress, which has its own rules and procedures. The Constitution also gives the House and Senate final say over whether to seat someone.
Here’s a look at what’s next and where issues could arise, aside from lawsuits that may be filed or already in progress.
When will there be official results?
Counting ballots and certifying the results takes at least a week in most states, often longer.
Kyle Yoder, research director at The Center for Election Innovation & Research, said that is exactly the type of deliberative process voters should want and expect. He also cautioned the results news organizations report in the hours and sometimes days after Nov. 3 aren’t final totals.
“Results aren’t official until every ballot has been counted by every eligible voter,” he said. “That process takes time, and when you sit back and think about it, you want it to take time because what we want is for that count to be correct, for it to be accurate, for it to be complete.”
Yoder added that the “biggest point of confusion that we run into when we’re talking to voters about all this is they think the results they’re seeing on their TV on election night are the final results.”
The Associated Press, which many news organizations look to for race calls, explains how its experts decide when to announce a winner and when to wait for more ballots to be counted. The Election Law Program, a collaborative effort between William & Mary Law School and the National Center for State Courts, has timelines for the various state deadlines.
How long can states take to recount ballots?
After election officials certify the first count of ballots, especially close races can head into a recount. Some state laws require it automatically if the margin of victory is under a certain percentage. In other circumstances, specific people can request a recount, typically the runner-up, though some state laws allow voters or even political parties to request another count.
“In many states, election recounts, legal challenges to the results, etcetera, can only begin once results have been certified,” Yoder said. “So it is in the interest of politicians who may be saber-rattling to allow certification to happen, so that they can begin those recounts, legal challenges.”
States have various deadlines for how long those recounts can last. But they can drag on amid lawsuits and Congress has the authority in some cases to conduct its own recount.

Late last year, a friend in Seattle suggested we train for an Ironman 70.3 from opposite coasts. He did the runs, swims, and bike rides along the Pacific Ocean, and I followed suit along the Chesapeake Bay. We weren’t sure whether we’d meet in the middle for an organized event in Nebraska, or save on travel costs with an unofficial “Do-It-Yourself” approach in our backyards.
About halfway through training, he dropped out because of a knee injury. I soldiered on. After 16 weeks of prep, I felt ready, so I set out on my own—no aid stations or medals waiting at the finish line—and accomplished the trek to Annapolis, Maryland, and back in the middle of a snowstorm, with 84 laps in the community pool counting as my 1.2-mile swim.
Later on, I moved to Jackson, Wyoming, where my runs, swims, and bike rides would take place in the shadow of the Tetons. I decided to increase my training workload to try for a full-distance Ironman, also DIY, in Grand Teton National Park. I doubled everything from the 70.3 training block except for the weekend long runs. The schedule as written would have quickly had me running marathons the day after punishing bike rides that took half a day and marked my longest-ever distances in the saddle.
It wasn’t easy. Trail runs and lake swims easily eclipsed the distances I’d done for my high school cross country and swim teams, respectively. And the time was hard to schedule around my 9-to-5. I found a few encouraging partners to swim, ride, and bike with, but I did the majority of the sessions on my own.
The joy of training in pristine wilderness, as spring turned to summer, turned out to be solid motivation. After missing only a handful of workouts over 16 weeks, I felt ready.
I had done another solo half-Ironman to get a feel for the course, my gear, and my fitness level. The week before my target DIY attempt on August 8, I raced a short gravel triathlon with some friends in Steamboat Springs, Colorado, placing second in the first-timers category.
An ill-fated first attempt
The week of my taper, I relaxed with virtually no workouts. On the day of my attempt, unfortunately, a thick smoke from a West Coast wildfire filled the valley. The swim felt fine, and the bike ride was issue-free, but I could feel my lungs working overtime. By the time I started the run, I couldn’t fathom the marathon ahead of me. The number International Business Machines (IBM) shareholders are watching comes from one business: its software. You may think of IBM as a consulting and hardware company, but its growth question lies in software. Yet over the year to November 3, 2026, IBM stock lost 16.5%, while the S&P 500 returned 11.9%. IBM’s software growth sped up in fiscal Q3 2026 anyway, and that is the contradiction. So how fast is IBM’s software growing now, and how much of it is new?
IBM’s Software Speed-Up Came Mostly From New Business
Measured at constant currency, IBM’s software revenue grew 9% in fiscal Q3 2026. That was four points faster than in Q2, management said on the October 21 call. Its high-value annual recurring revenue base, software sales that repeat each year, grew 8% to $24.9 billion.
Some of a jump like that can be borrowed from the quarter before, and IBM did close about two-thirds of the large deals that slipped out of Q2. Management, however, put those deals at about a quarter of the speed-up and called about three-quarters of it net new business. Based on management’s own split, most of the gain was not catch-up.
Can IBM’s Software Growth Hold As Mainframe Software Cools?
Management said not all of that growth will hold. The company does not expect transaction processing, the software that runs on its mainframes, to keep growing at double digits, and said it could perhaps moderate from Q3 into Q4. So more of the growth has to come from the rest of IBM’s software, such as Red Hat, and so far Red Hat is holding up.
That matters because software license deals have already swung IBM’s software growth once. In fiscal Q2 2026, management said, a double-digit fall in transactional software sales, which make up about a fifth of its software business, cut software growth by 4 to 5 points. In Q3, those sales rose by double digits, mostly in transaction processing, which grew 10%.
Red Hat looks steadier. Its revenue grew 11% in fiscal Q3 2026, the same rate as the quarter before, and its bookings growth sped up to the high teens. OpenShift, a Red Hat product, is now a $2.4 billion annual recurring revenue business, growing more than 30%.
What Would Show IBM’s Software Growth Fading?
From the 9% alone, you cannot tell how much of IBM’s software growth will repeat. Part of it came from deals that slipped out of Q2, and the double-digit rise in mainframe software is the part management expects to fade. If the new business does not repeat, the speed-up was a one-quarter jump. If Red Hat does not grow into the gap, IBM’s software growth again swings with mainframe deals.
Management has said little about 2027 so far. When Red Hat’s bookings and 2027 came up on the October call, management declined to comment on 2027 growth. Later in the call, it gave only an early view that growth would speed back up to its model. It did say bookings growth of this kind usually turns into good revenue growth.
So far, management credits most of IBM’s software speed-up to new business, and Red Hat’s bookings are growing faster than they were. Since management expects mainframe software to cool, Red Hat’s ability to grow into the gap is the open question. IBM’s software growth, along with Red Hat’s part in it, is the number to watch when IBM reports in January 2027. Management has said it will put figures on 2027 then.

Pricing power means a company can charge more for what it sells and its customers keep buying. When ingredients, packaging and freight get more expensive, a company with pricing power passes those costs on, protects its margins and keeps enough profit coming in to raise its dividend. Consumer prices rose 3.7% year over year in the latest CPI reading, and any income stream that stays flat loses buying power while inflation stays that high. Colgate-Palmolive: Higher Prices and More Units Sold
Colgate sells everyday basics to households worldwide: Colgate toothpaste, Palmolive and Irish Spring soap, Speed Stick deodorant, Fabuloso cleaner, Tom’s of Maine, and Hill’s pet food. People buy these cheap items repeatedly as part of their daily routine. That gives the company room to raise prices a little at a time.
Evidence of pricing power: Organic sales rose 3.6% in the third quarter. Pricing added 2.0% and volume added 1.7%, so Colgate charged more and sold more units in the same quarter. Two weeks out from my first marathon, I looked in the mirror and didn’t see the version of myself I thought I would. There was no six-pack, not even a hint of ab definition. My glutes weren’t particularly sculpted, and I wouldn’t exactly describe myself as lean like many runners I see.
At 5-foot-10, I’ve never been the smallest girl in the room. And while my long legs certainly help me cover more distance, I expected months of marathon training to leave me looking more visibly athletic, with more muscle definition and a physique that reflected just how hard I’d been working. I thought that after months of early alarms, added protein, and steadily increasing mileage, I’d look in the mirror and see a different body type.
Somewhere along the way, I absorbed the idea that a runner’s body should look a certain way. When mine didn’t match that image, I started wondering if I wasn’t training hard enough, if I was doing something wrong, or if my body simply wasn’t responding the way it was supposed to.
As I approached race day, I thought about why I was holding myself to that standard in the first place, especially because I was running the New York City Marathon on behalf of Planned Parenthood of Greater New York, an organization whose work centers on bodily autonomy and compassionate care.
Why was I putting so much pressure on my body to look different when it was already doing something incredible? I realized training for a marathon isn’t just about building endurance; it can also mean confronting the expectations you place on yourself.
Where Does the Idea of a ‘Runner’s Body’ Come From?
So many people have an idea of what a “runner’s body” is supposed to look like, particularly fed by what we see online. When you see the same body type represented over and over, it’s easy to start associating that appearance with athleticism. What's your first thought when you see "half off" at the bakery? Are you eager to snap up a quick deal, or do you assume the bread's gone stale? A similar question emerges in the stock market.
Take Salesforce (CRM +2.21%), for example. The company's stock has endured a rough patch over the last two years. At its June 2026 low, the stock had dropped more than 59% from its all-time high.
But to decide whether Salesforce is a ready-made bargain or a week-old baguette, we need to examine the details.
Salesforce's 50% stock declines are rare
Salesforce has been a public company since 2004. In its more than 22 years as a public company, its stock has dropped 50% or more from its all-time high on only three occasions:
- Oct. 7, 2008: Salesforce stock fell sharply, along with the broader market, as the financial crisis shook Wall Street. Salesforce stock ultimately declined by 70% before bottoming in November 2008.
- Sept. 1, 2022: Salesforce stock melted slowly throughout late 2021 and nearly all of 2022 during the latest bear market. After crossing the 50% threshold in September 2022, the stock bottomed in December 2022, down 59% from its all-time high, before recovering and setting new all-time highs in 2024.
- Feb. 23, 2026: Salesforce stock fell below the 50% mark in February 2026 as market participants fretted over whether software-as-a-service (SaaS) business models would withstand rapid innovations in the artificial intelligence (AI) sector.
These drops aren't garden-variety pullbacks; they are rare structural resets. And in the latest case, a recovery may already be underway.
Past recoveries rewarded patience, not perfect timing
So, let's see what happened in the past. In each case, we'll assume an investor bought the day after the 50% level was crossed. In the 2008 case, shares gained 63% in the year after the breach. In 2022, Salesforce stock rose 44% in the following 12 months. However, there's one very important caveat: Things got worse before they got better. In 2008, shares dropped another 39% before the bottom was truly in. In 2022, shares fell another 16%.
In other words, while a 50% drop is massive for Salesforce stock, investors shouldn't think of it as a line in the sand. The stock can -- and has -- fallen even further before. Past rebounds show resilience, but today's recovery requires a clear-eyed look at the current business.

As President Donald Trump campaigned for the nation's highest office in 2024, he regularly blamed Democrats for the country's economic anxiety.
During campaign stops across the U.S., Trump frequently asked voters if they were better off than they were four years prior. At the time, his message appeared to land: In an election centered on inflation and the cost of living, Trump won every swing state and the nationwide popular vote.
Two years later, voters grappling with those same kitchen-table issues took away much of his party's power in Washington and in states across the country.
Democrats rode a blue wave of historic proportions in Tuesday's midterm election to flip everything from battleground congressional seats to long-held Republican governorships. The Democratic Party will now have control of both the House and Senate, ending the Republican Party's trifecta of power in the federal government.
Nearly nine out of 10 voters in the CNBC Voter Poll said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress. Participants in the poll ranked the economy as the most important issue facing the country during the midterm election, ahead of topics like the state of democracy and immigration. Three out of every four survey participants rated the economy as "poor" or "not so good," compared with just 2% who described it as "excellent."
And perhaps most telling of all: Fewer than one out of every five voters said their family's financial standing was better than it was two years ago.
Much of their dissatisfaction was centered on Trump himself, with about two out of every three voters saying his policies worsened economic conditions in the country.
"It was all about the economy," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "Most Americans are struggling with the high inflation and have been for quite some time, and they're just angry."
A 'breaking point'
Tuesday's election played out against the backdrop of a war with Iran that has been politically unpopular and exacerbated the inflationary pressures facing everyday Americans. The CNBC Voter Poll found nearly three out of every four people said the war was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.
Trump told Fox News that voters were presumably unhappy with the surge in gas prices, even if they generally agreed with the need for military action against Iran. Vice President JD Vance said on social media that some voters who backed him and Trump in 2024 likely supported Democrats in the midterms as a result of the war.
U.S. drivers paid about $4.15 for an average gallon of gas on Tuesday, the highest of any midterm or presidential election day since at least 2000, according to AAA. Gas prices have surged about 37% over the past year as the Middle East conflict crippled the global crude trade.
